questions.q: According to Tom Mitchell's (1998) definition, a computer program learns from experience E with respect to task T and performance measure P if what happens?
o: Its performance on T stays constant regardless of E
Its performance on T, as measured by P, improves with experience E
It is explicitly programmed to perform T
It memorises all examples in E
questions.e: Tom Mitchell's definition: a computer program is said to learn from experience E with respect to some task T and some performance measure P, if its performance on T, as measured by P, improves with experience E.

questions.q: Who defined machine learning as 'the field of study that gives computers the ability to learn without being explicitly programmed', and in what year?
o: Tom Mitchell, 1998
Arthur Samuel, 1959
Andrew Ng, 2011
Ethem Alpaydin, 2004
questions.e: Arthur Samuel (1959) defined machine learning as the field of study that gives computers the ability to learn without being explicitly programmed.

questions.q: For the checkers-playing learning problem (T = play checkers, P = % of games won, E = opportunity to play against itself), what does P represent?
o: The task of playing checkers
The performance measure — the percentage of games won in a tournament
The training experience
The number of pieces on the board
questions.e: In the checkers example, T is the task (play checkers), P is the performance measure (percentage of games won in a tournament), and E is the training experience (the opportunity to play against itself).

questions.q: What is the relationship between artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML)?
o: ML is broader than AI
ML is a subset of AI; AI is the goal (make machines intelligent) and ML is the method (use data to learn and improve)
They are the same thing
AI is a subset of ML
questions.e: AI is a broad field focused on building systems that perform tasks requiring human-like intelligence; ML is a subset of AI focused on algorithms and statistical models that learn patterns from data. AI is the goal (make machines intelligent), and ML is the method (use data to learn and improve).

questions.q: What is emphasised as the most important aspect of learning, illustrated by recognising trucks and dumpers beyond the training examples?
o: Memorising every training example exactly
The ability to generalize from labeled examples to new, unseen cases
Using the fastest possible algorithm
Collecting the largest possible dataset
questions.e: Learning involves the ability to generalize from labeled examples; the goal is that after learning from examples the system can correctly recognise new, previously unseen cases.

questions.q: In the components of a predictor (question → input data → features → algorithm → parameters → evaluation), what is the stated relative order of importance?
o: algorithms > features > data > question
question > data > features > algorithms
features > algorithms > question > data
data > algorithms > question > features
questions.e: The relative order of importance is: a concrete/specific question > relevant data > properly extracted features > algorithms. Getting the question and data right matters more than the choice of algorithm.

questions.q: What does the phrase 'garbage in = garbage out' express about data selection in machine learning?
o: That algorithms are more important than data
That having the correct/relevant data determines whether the model is successful — poor input data yields poor output
That more complex algorithms always help
That data should be discarded before modelling
questions.e: 'Garbage in = garbage out' means that having the correct and relevant data decides whether the model is successful; if the input data is poor, the model's output will be poor no matter the algorithm. More relevant data usually gives better models.

questions.q: The Google Flu Trends example is used to illustrate what pitfall of prediction?
o: That prediction is always impossible
That a model can fail to predict accurately when the underlying behavior (people's search habits) changes
That flu cannot be modelled
That algorithms are unimportant
questions.e: Google Flu failed to predict accurately when people's search habits changed, illustrating the importance of choosing the right dataset and understanding what the specific question is — models can break when the underlying behavior shifts.

questions.q: In the credit-scoring example, the discriminant 'IF income > θ1 AND savings > θ2 THEN low-risk ELSE high-risk' is an example of what kind of ML task?
o: Regression
Clustering
A classification rule that separates low-risk from high-risk customers
Reinforcement learning
questions.e: The credit-scoring discriminant classifies customers as low-risk or high-risk based on thresholds for income and savings; it is a classification rule that differentiates between the two categories.

questions.q: Prediction is described as being fundamentally about what?
o: Always choosing the most complex algorithm
Finding the correct balance among trade-offs such as interpretability, accuracy, speed, simplicity, and scalability
Collecting as much data as possible only
Avoiding any evaluation
questions.e: Prediction is about trade-offs: finding the correct balance between interpretability, accuracy, speed, simplicity, and scalability. Interpretability is important for conveying how features predict the outcome, and scalability is important for practical use on large datasets.

questions.q: The ALVINN system, cited as an autonomous-driving application, was based on what and could do what?
o: A decision tree; parked cars
A neural network (Autonomous Land Vehicle In a Neural Network); it drove 70 mph on highways
A support vector machine; recognised faces
A clustering algorithm; sorted images
questions.e: ALVINN (Autonomous Land Vehicle In a Neural Network) was a neural-network-based system that drove at 70 mph on highways, cited as an early autonomous-driving application.

questions.q: The general process for prediction moves through which sequence?
o: Evaluate → predict → build → sample → population
Population → probability/sampling to pick data → split into training and test set → build prediction function → predict for new data → evaluate
Build → deploy → forget
Features → algorithm → question → data
questions.e: The prediction process is: start from a population, use probability and sampling to pick a set of data, split it into training and test sets, build a prediction function, predict for new data, and then evaluate.

questions.q: What is a feature in machine learning, and what is a feature vector?
o: A feature is the model's output; a feature vector is the error
A feature is an individual measurable property (independent variable/attribute) of the observed signal; the set of features used for learning is called the feature vector
A feature is a training algorithm; a feature vector is a test set
A feature is a class label; a feature vector is a single number
questions.e: A feature is an individual measurable property of the signal being observed — an independent variable or column/attribute of the data (e.g. number of rooms, size of a house). The set of features used for learning/recognition is called the feature vector.

questions.q: What is the dimensionality of a dataset, and what does dimensionality reduction do?
o: The number of rows; it removes rows
The number of input variables (features); dimensionality reduction reduces the number of input variables, which can help because large numbers of features can cause poor performance
The number of classes; it merges classes
The size of the test set; it enlarges it
questions.e: The dimensionality of a dataset is the number of input variables (features). Dimensionality reduction refers to techniques that reduce the number of input variables, which helps because large numbers of input features can cause poor performance for ML algorithms.

questions.q: What makes a 'good' feature for classification?
o: Objects from the same class have very different feature values
Objects from the same class have similar feature values, and objects from different classes have different values
The feature has as many distinct values as possible
The feature is randomly generated
questions.e: Good features are those where objects from the same class have similar feature values, while objects from different classes have different values; such discriminative features are good for learning.

questions.q: What are the three main types of machine learning?
o: Linear, polynomial, and logistic
Supervised learning, unsupervised learning, and reinforcement learning
Classification, regression, and clustering
Training, validation, and testing
questions.e: The three main types of machine learning are supervised learning (which includes classification and regression), unsupervised learning, and reinforcement learning.

questions.q: What is the key difference between classification and regression?
o: Classification predicts a continuous variable; regression predicts a discrete one
Classification predicts a discrete (categorical) variable, while regression predicts a continuous variable
They are identical
Classification is unsupervised; regression is supervised
questions.e: In classification, the variable we are trying to predict is discrete (a category); in regression, the variable we are trying to predict is continuous. Both are supervised learning tasks.

questions.q: What does a classifier do in feature space?
o: It generates new features
It partitions the feature space into class-labeled regions; classification determines to which region a feature vector belongs, and the borders between regions are called decision boundaries
It removes outliers from the data
It computes the mean of all features
questions.e: A classifier partitions the feature space into class-labeled regions; classification consists of determining to which region a feature vector belongs, and the borders between regions are called decision boundaries.

questions.q: How is supervised learning best described?
o: Letting the computer find patterns on its own with no labels
Teaching the computer with labeled examples (data with known answers), so it learns to predict or classify new, unseen data — like a teacher guiding a student with correct answers
Learning by trial and error with rewards and punishments
Grouping data into clusters
questions.e: Supervised learning is like teaching with examples: you give the computer data with known answers (labeled data), and it learns patterns to make predictions or classifications on new, unseen data, like a teacher guiding a student with the correct answers.

questions.q: How is unsupervised learning described?
o: Teaching with labeled examples
The computer is left to find patterns and relationships in data on its own, without being told the answers — like assembling a puzzle without knowing the final picture
Learning from rewards and punishments
Predicting a continuous value
questions.e: In unsupervised learning, the computer is left to find patterns and relationships in the data on its own, without labels — like being given a pile of mixed-up puzzle pieces and figuring out how they fit without being told what the final picture looks like. Clustering is a key example.

questions.q: What is the principle behind clustering?
o: Maximising inter-cluster similarity and minimising intra-cluster similarity
Maximising intra-cluster similarity and minimising inter-cluster similarity (points in the same group are similar, points in different groups are dissimilar)
Assigning every point to one label given in advance
Predicting a continuous target value
questions.e: Clustering groups data to form new categories (clusters) on the principle of maximizing intra-cluster similarity (points within a cluster are similar) and minimizing inter-cluster similarity (points in different clusters are dissimilar).

questions.q: The 'cocktail party effect' — separating independent sources from a mixed signal — is solved using which technique, and how does it differ from PCA?
o: Decision trees; it maximises variance
Independent Component Analysis (ICA); unlike PCA, which maximises the variance of the data, ICA focuses on independence (independent components)
K-means; it minimises distance
Naive Bayes; it uses probabilities
questions.e: The cocktail party effect is addressed by Independent Component Analysis (ICA), a technique to separate independent sources from a mixed signal; unlike principal component analysis (PCA), which focuses on maximizing the variance of the data, ICA focuses on independence — separating independent components.

questions.q: What are the two challenges of classification versus clustering illustrated by 'the letter T in different typefaces' and 'characters that look similar'?
o: Overfitting and underfitting
Intra-class variability (objects in the same class vary, e.g. T in different fonts) and inter-class similarity (objects in different classes look similar, e.g. similar characters or identical twins)
Bias and variance
Precision and recall
questions.e: The two challenges are intra-class variability — objects within the same class can look very different (the letter T in different typefaces, the same face under different poses) — and inter-class similarity — objects from different classes can look similar (characters that look alike, identical twins).

questions.q: How is reinforcement learning best described?
o: Learning from labeled examples provided by a teacher
The computer is given a goal and learns to achieve it through trial-and-error interactions with its environment, learning from success and failure via reward and punishment
Grouping unlabeled data into clusters
Predicting a continuous value from features
questions.e: In reinforcement learning, the computer is given a goal and learns how to achieve it by trial-and-error interactions with its environment; the system learns from success and failure, reward and punishment — similar to training a pet dog with 'good dog' and 'bad dog'.

questions.q: In the fish-sorting (salmon vs sea bass) example, why is using an overly complex model to draw the decision boundary a problem?
o: It is too simple to separate the classes
It leads to complicated decision boundaries that may perfectly classify the training samples but perform poorly on future patterns — overfitting (poor generalization)
It cannot use any features
It always minimises the risk
questions.e: An overly complex model produces complicated decision boundaries; while it may give zero classification error on the training samples, it performs poorly on future patterns because generalization is poor — this is overfitting. Occam's Razor suggests simpler models should be preferred over complex ones.

questions.q: What is generalization error, and what does Occam's Razor recommend?
o: Error on the training set; prefer complex models

The classification error on the test (unseen) data — minimizing error on the training set does not guarantee minimizing it on test data; Occam's Razor recommends preferring simpler models over complex ones
The error before training; prefer larger datasets
The number of features; prefer more features
questions.e: Generalization error is the classification error on the test database; minimizing the classification error on the training database does not guarantee minimizing the generalization error. Occam's Razor principle says that simpler models should be preferred over complex ones.

questions.q: What is data preprocessing, and why is it needed?
o: Deploying the final model; because models are complex

The process of preparing raw data and making it suitable for a machine learning model (the first and crucial step); it is needed because real-world data generally contains noise, missing values, and may be in an unusable format
Training the model; because data is always clean
Evaluating the model; because metrics vary
questions.e: Data preprocessing is the process of preparing raw data and making it suitable for a machine learning model; it is the first and crucial step. It is needed because real-world data generally contains noise and missing values and may be in an unusable format that cannot be directly used.

questions.q: Which set correctly lists key steps of data preprocessing?
o: Train, validate, test, deploy
Acquire the dataset, import libraries, import the dataset, identify and handle missing values, encode categorical data, split the dataset, and feature scaling
Question, data, features, algorithm, parameters
Sensing, segmentation, feature extraction, classification
questions.e: The steps for data preprocessing are: acquire the dataset, import the crucial libraries, import the dataset, identify and handle missing values, encode the categorical data, split the dataset, and perform feature scaling.

questions.q: Which Python libraries are used, respectively, for scientific calculation/arrays, data manipulation/importing datasets, and 2D plotting?
o: Pandas, Numpy, Seaborn
Numpy, Pandas, Matplotlib
Scikit-learn, TensorFlow, Keras
Matplotlib, Numpy, Pandas
questions.e: Numpy is the fundamental package for scientific calculation (arrays and matrices), Pandas is the open-source library for data manipulation and analysis (importing and managing datasets), and Matplotlib is the 2D plotting library used to plot charts.

questions.q: What are the two commonly used methods for handling missing values?
o: Encoding and scaling
Deleting a particular row (or column) and imputing the data (replacing with the mean, median, most frequent value, or a constant)
Training and testing
Binning and normalization
questions.e: The two commonly used methods for handling missing data are deleting a particular row (or a column where more than 75% of values are missing) and imputing the data — replacing missing values with the mean, median, most frequently occurring value, or a constant value.

questions.q: What is the difference between ordinal-data mapping and one-hot (dummy) encoding for categorical data?
o: Ordinal mapping is for nominal data; one-hot is for ordinal data

Ordinal mapping is used when order matters (mapping categories to ordered numbers); one-hot/dummy encoding is used for nominal (unordered) data, creating 0/1 dummy variables so the model does not assume a false ordering
They are identical
Ordinal mapping creates dummy variables; one-hot preserves order
questions.e: Ordinal-data mapping is used when order matters, mapping categories to ordered numbers (e.g. not satisfied=0, satisfied=1, very satisfied=3). One-hot (dummy) encoding is used for nominal data, which has no order; it creates dummy variables taking values 0 or 1, so the model does not wrongly assume a correlation/order among the categories. The number of columns equals the number of categories.

questions.q: What are the two common train/test split ratios, and what does the training set contain?
o: 50:50 and 60:40; the training set has no known outputs
70:30 and 80:20; the training set is the subset used to train the model, where the output is already known
90:10 and 95:5; the training set is used only for testing
10:90 and 20:80; the training set is the largest
questions.e: The dataset is usually split in a 70:30 or 80:20 ratio (training:test). The training set is the subset used for training the model, where the output is already known; the test set is used to predict outcomes and evaluate the trained model.

questions.q: What is feature scaling, and why is it needed?
o: Increasing the number of features; to add complexity

A method to standardize (limit the range of) the independent variables so they can be compared on common grounds, preventing algorithms from being influenced by higher-valued features (e.g. salary dominating age)
Removing features; to reduce dimensionality
Splitting the dataset; to create a test set
questions.e: Feature scaling is a method to standardize the independent variables within a specific range so they can be compared on common grounds; it prevents algorithms from being influenced by higher values (e.g. if age and salary are on different scales, salary values would dominate and give incorrect results).

questions.q: What is the difference between normalization (min-max) and standardization?
o: Normalization sets mean=0, std=1; standardization rescales to [0,1]
Normalization rescales values into the range [0,1] (outliers can be lost), while standardization rescales the data so that the mean = 0 and the standard deviation = 1
They are identical
Normalization is applied column-wise; standardization row-wise
questions.e: Normalization (min-max) rescales values into the range [0,1], and outliers from the dataset can be lost; standardization rescales the data so that the mean = 0 and the standard deviation = 1.

questions.q: What is data binning (bucketing), and what are its main approaches?
o: Deleting bins of data; by row and by column

Grouping data into bins/buckets, replacing values in a small interval with a single representative value; approaches include binning by distance, binning by frequency, and binning by sampling (mean, median, or boundary)
Splitting data into train and test
Encoding categorical variables
questions.e: Data binning (bucketing) groups data into bins/buckets, replacing values in a small interval with a single representative value; it can convert numeric to categorical values. Approaches include binning by distance, binning by frequency (each bin has ~the same number of observations), and binning by sampling (by mean, median, or boundary value).

questions.q: Data binning is one of three techniques used for data smoothing (removing noise from data). What are the other two?
o: Encoding and scaling
Regression and outlier analysis
Training and testing
Sampling and quantization
questions.e: Data smoothing is employed to remove noise from data; the three techniques used are binning, regression, and outlier analysis.

questions.q: What is regression analysis?
o: A method for grouping unlabeled data into clusters
A statistical method that analyzes and understands the relationship between two or more variables, forecasting a dependent variable (Y) from one or more independent variables (X)
A way to reduce dimensionality
A method that predicts discrete categories only
questions.e: Regression analysis is a statistical method that helps analyze and understand the relationship between two or more variables; it normally has one dependent variable and one or more independent variables, and forecasts the value of the dependent variable Y from the independent variables X.

questions.q: In the simple linear regression model y = b0 + b1*x, what do b0 and b1 represent?
o: b0 is the slope and b1 is the intercept
b0 is the y-intercept and b1 is the slope of the line
b0 is the error and b1 is the dependent variable
b0 and b1 are both errors
questions.e: In y = b0 + b1*x, y is the dependent variable, x is the independent variable, b0 is the y-intercept, and b1 is the slope of the line; we need to find b0 and b1 to estimate y such that the error is minimized.

questions.q: The Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) method finds the best line by doing what?
o: Maximising the sum of squared differences
Minimizing the sum of squared differences (squared residuals) between the data points and the line
Minimizing the number of features
Maximising the number of data points on the line
questions.e: Ordinary least squares (OLS) is used to implement simple linear regression; a good line is one that minimizes the sum of squared differences between the points and the line. Each squared residual is the vertical distance between a data point and the fitted line, and the goal is to make the sum of these squared deviations as small as possible.

questions.q: What are the four assumptions of simple linear regression?
o: Speed, accuracy, simplicity, and scalability
Homoscedasticity (equal spread of errors), independence of observations, normality (of residuals), and linearity
Bias, variance, precision, and recall
Mean, median, mode, and range
questions.e: Simple linear regression is a parametric test that assumes: homoscedasticity (the errors have about the same spread regardless of the input value), independence of observations, normality (the errors/residuals follow a normal distribution), and linearity (a straight-line relationship). If homoscedasticity or normality is violated, a nonparametric test such as the Spearman rank test may be used.

questions.q: What is multiple linear regression (MLR)?
o: Regression with a single independent variable
Regression used to estimate the relationship between two or more independent variables and one dependent variable
Regression that predicts categories
Regression with no dependent variable
questions.e: Multiple linear regression is used to estimate the relationship between two or more independent variables and one dependent variable, e.g. how rainfall, temperature, and fertilizer together affect crop growth; its formula is y = B0 + B1X1 + ... + BnXn + e.

questions.q: In multiple linear regression, what do a large T-score and a small p-value (below ~0.05) indicate about an independent variable?
o: That the variable is not a significant predictor
That the variable is a statistically significant predictor with a meaningful impact on the dependent variable
That the variable should be removed
That the model is overfitting
questions.e: A large T-score means the variable has a stronger influence on the dependent variable, and a small p-value (typically below 0.05) means the relationship is unlikely to have occurred by chance — together they indicate the variable is a statistically significant predictor. Small T-scores and large p-values suggest a variable is not a significant predictor.

questions.q: In hypothesis testing (e.g. the coin-toss example), what is the p-value?
o: The probability that the alternative hypothesis is false
The lowest significance level that results in rejecting the null hypothesis; a smaller p-value indicates a more significant relationship
The number of coin tosses
The mean of the errors
questions.e: The p-value is the lowest significance level that results in rejecting the null hypothesis; a smaller p-value indicates a more significant relationship between the independent and dependent variables. In the coin-toss example, once the p-value drops below the 5% threshold, the null hypothesis (fair coin) is rejected.

questions.q: Why is polynomial regression used, and what problem does it address?
o: To reduce the number of features; overfitting
It adds powers of the original features to increase model complexity, addressing under-fitting when a straight line cannot capture the patterns in the data
To make the model linear; multicollinearity
To remove outliers; missing data
questions.e: Polynomial regression is used to overcome under-fitting, where a straight line is unable to capture the patterns in the data; to increase model complexity, powers of the original features are added as new features, generating a higher-order equation.

questions.q: What is the bias-variance trade-off?
o: Bias is error from complexity; variance is error from simplicity

Bias is the error from a model's simplistic assumptions (high bias causes under-fitting); variance is the error from an overly complex model (high variance causes over-fitting). As complexity increases, bias decreases and variance increases; the ideal model has low bias and low variance
Bias and variance are always equal
Bias applies to training; variance to testing only
questions.e: Bias refers to the error due to a model's simplistic assumptions — high bias means the model cannot capture the patterns, causing under-fitting. Variance refers to the error due to a complex model fitting the data too closely — high variance causes over-fitting. As model complexity increases, bias decreases and variance increases; ideally a model has both low bias and low variance, but a trade-off must be made.

questions.q: What does R-squared (R²) measure in regression model evaluation?
o: The number of independent variables
The explained variance divided by the total variance
The sum of squared errors only
The slope of the regression line
questions.e: R² = Explained variance / Total variance; the explained variance is the sum of squared differences between the predicted values and the mean of the dependent variable, and the total variance is the sum of squared differences between the actual values and the mean.

questions.q: For the least-squares example fitting the points (0,2),(1,3),(2,5),(3,4),(4,6), the regression line is y = 0.9x + 2.2. What are the slope and intercept?
o: Slope 2.2, intercept 0.9
Slope 0.9, intercept 2.2
Slope 0.5, intercept 4.0
Slope 1.0, intercept 3.0
questions.e: For y = 0.9x + 2.2, the slope (a) is 0.9 and the y-intercept (b) is 2.2, computed using the least-squares regression formulas from the tabulated sums.

questions.q: When distinguishing 'linear' from 'non-linear' regression models, what relationship is actually being described as linear?
o: The relationship between y and the powers of x
The relationship between y and the coefficients (b's) is linear, since there are no b² or b³ terms
The relationship between the features
The relationship between training and test sets
questions.e: When distinguishing linear and non-linear regression models, we are not talking about the relationship between y and the x-terms (which may include powers), but about the relationship between y and the coefficients (b's), which is linear because there are no b² or b³ terms.

questions.q: What is a confusion matrix?
o: A list of all features in a model
An N×N table that summarizes a classification model's predictions, with one axis the predicted label and the other the actual label (for binary classification N=2)
A plot of training error over time
The set of decision boundaries
questions.e: A confusion matrix is an N×N table that summarizes how successful a classification model's predictions were — the correlation between the actual label and the model's classification. One axis is the predicted label and the other is the actual label; N is the number of classes, so for binary classification N=2.

questions.q: In a confusion matrix, what is a false negative (FN)?
o: An observation predicted positive that was actually positive
An observation predicted negative that was actually positive (the model missed a real positive)
An observation predicted positive that was actually negative
An observation predicted negative that was actually negative
questions.e: A false negative (FN) is the number of observations the model predicted as negative that were actually positive — a missed positive (e.g. missing a cancer case or a landmine). A false positive (FP) is predicted positive but actually negative.

questions.q: How is accuracy defined, and why can it be a poor metric?
o: Accuracy = TP/(TP+FP); it is always the best metric

Accuracy = (correctly classified instances)/(total instances); it can be misleading for imbalanced datasets (e.g. 90 healthy and 10 sick, classifying everyone healthy gives 90% accuracy while missing all sick people)
Accuracy = TP/(TP+FN); it works only for regression
Accuracy = TN/(TN+FP); it is unaffected by imbalance
questions.e: Accuracy is the number of correctly classified instances over the total number of instances. It can be a poor metric when the dataset is imbalanced: with 90 healthy and 10 sick people, a model that classifies everyone as healthy achieves 90% accuracy while completely failing to identify any sick person.

questions.q: How are precision and recall defined?
o: Precision = TP/(TP+FN); Recall = TP/(TP+FP)
Precision = TP/(TP+FP) (of predicted positives, how many are correct); Recall = TP/(TP+FN) (of actual positives, how many are detected)
Precision = TN/(TN+FP); Recall = TN/(TN+FN)
They are the same quantity
questions.e: Precision is the ratio of correctly classified positive samples (TP) to the total predicted positive (TP+FP); it becomes 1 when FP = 0. Recall is the ratio of correctly classified positives (TP) to the total actual positives (TP+FN); it measures the ability to detect positive samples and becomes 1 when FN = 0.

questions.q: What is the F1 score?
o: The arithmetic mean of accuracy and precision
The harmonic mean of precision and recall; it is high only when both precision and recall are high, and is considered a better measure than accuracy
The ratio of true negatives to all negatives
The area under the ROC curve
questions.e: The F1 score is the harmonic mean of precision and recall; it becomes 1 only when both precision and recall are 1, and it becomes high only when both are high. It is considered a better measure than accuracy, especially for imbalanced data.

questions.q: How are sensitivity and specificity defined?
o: Sensitivity = TN/(TN+FP); Specificity = TP/(TP+FN)
Sensitivity = TP/(TP+FN) (True Positive Rate, also called recall); Specificity = TN/(TN+FP) (True Negative Rate)
Both equal TP/(TP+FP)
Sensitivity is precision; Specificity is accuracy
questions.e: Sensitivity = TP/(TP+FN) is the True Positive Rate (also known as recall) — the proportion of actual positives predicted correctly. Specificity = TN/(TN+FP) is the True Negative Rate — the proportion of actual negatives predicted correctly.

questions.q: What does 100% specificity mean for a test?
o: It detects all positive cases but with many false positives
It produces no false positives, but may miss some positive cases
It always misclassifies negatives
It has zero true negatives
questions.e: 100% specificity means the test produces no false positives, but it may miss some positive cases (e.g. some cancer cases). By contrast, 100% sensitivity detects all positive cases but possibly with many false positives.

questions.q: On an ROC curve, TP rate is plotted against FP rate. What does a curve closer to the top-left corner indicate, and what does the diagonal represent?
o: Top-left indicates worse performance; the diagonal is perfect

A curve closer to the top-left corner indicates better performance; the 45-degree diagonal (FPR = TPR) represents a random classifier — the closer the curve is to the diagonal, the less accurate the test
Top-left indicates random guessing; the diagonal is perfect classification
Both indicate identical performance
questions.e: In ROC space, TP rate is on the Y axis and FP rate on the X axis; classifiers giving curves closer to the top-left corner indicate better performance. A random classifier is expected to give points along the 45-degree diagonal (FPR = TPR), and the closer the curve comes to that diagonal, the less accurate the test. The point (0,1) represents perfect classification.

questions.q: What is the AUC (Area Under the ROC Curve), and what statistical property does it have?
o: The area of the confusion matrix; it equals accuracy

The area under the ROC curve; it equals the probability that the classifier will rank a randomly chosen positive instance higher than a randomly chosen negative instance — the bigger the AUC, the better
The number of true positives; higher is worse
The slope of the ROC curve; it equals recall
questions.e: The AUC (Area Under the ROC Curve) has the statistical property that it equals the probability the classifier will rank a randomly chosen positive instance higher than a randomly chosen negative instance; it is often used to compare classifiers, and the bigger the AUC, the better.

questions.q: In ROC space, how are 'conservative' and 'liberal' classifiers characterised?
o: Conservative classifiers have high false-positive rates; liberal ones have low

Conservative classifiers (left, near the X axis) make positive classifications only with strong evidence, giving few false positives but often low true-positive rates; liberal classifiers (upper right) classify positives with weak evidence, catching nearly all positives but with high false-positive rates
Conservative and liberal classifiers perform identically
Conservative classifiers are always below the diagonal
questions.e: Conservative classifiers appear on the left of the ROC graph near the X axis; they make positive classifications only with strong evidence, so they make few false-positive errors but often have low true-positive rates. Liberal classifiers appear on the upper right; they make positive classifications with weak evidence, classifying nearly all positives correctly but with high false-positive rates.

questions.q: In a multi-class confusion matrix, what do the diagonal and off-diagonal values represent?
o: Diagonal = incorrect predictions; off-diagonal = correct predictions
Diagonal values represent correct predictions (predicted class matches actual class); off-diagonal values represent incorrect predictions
Both represent correct predictions
Diagonal = precision; off-diagonal = recall
questions.e: In a multi-class confusion matrix (N×N, where N is the number of classes), each row is the actual class and each column the predicted class; diagonal values represent correct predictions (predicted class matches actual class), and off-diagonal values represent incorrect predictions.

questions.q: What is the fundamental assumption made by a Naive Bayes classifier?
o: That features are strongly dependent on each other
That each feature makes an independent and equal contribution to the outcome
That the data is always normally distributed
That there is only one feature
questions.e: The fundamental Naive Bayes assumption is that each feature makes an independent contribution to the outcome and an equal contribution to the outcome; it is a classification technique based on Bayes' Theorem.

questions.q: Bayes' Theorem is written as which of the following?
o: P(A|B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A and B)
P(A|B) = P(B|A) * P(A) / P(B)
P(A|B) = P(A) * P(B)
P(A|B) = P(B|A) / P(A)
questions.e: Bayes' Theorem is P(A|B) = P(B|A) * P(A) / P(B); Naive Bayes is a probabilistic machine learning model for classification based on this theorem.

questions.q: Which type of Naive Bayes classifier is commonly used for text classification with discrete word-count features?
o: Gaussian Naive Bayes
Multinomial Naive Bayes
Bernoulli Naive Bayes
Linear Naive Bayes
questions.e: Multinomial Naive Bayes is commonly used for text classification tasks (such as spam detection or document categorization); it is suited for data with discrete features like word counts, modelling each term as a multinomial distribution.

questions.q: Which Naive Bayes variant assumes continuous features follow a normal (Gaussian) distribution?
o: Multinomial Naive Bayes
Bernoulli Naive Bayes
Gaussian Naive Bayes
Poisson Naive Bayes
questions.e: Gaussian Naive Bayes is suitable for classification where features are continuous and follow a Gaussian (normal) distribution; it uses the mean and standard deviation to model the distribution (giving a bell-shaped curve). Bernoulli Naive Bayes is used for binary present/absent features.

questions.q: What is the difference between prior and posterior probability in Naive Bayes?
o: Prior is calculated after data; posterior before
The prior probability is the probability of an event before new data is collected; the posterior probability is the probability of the hypothesis being true in the light of the observed data
They are identical
Prior applies to features; posterior to labels only
questions.e: The prior probability is the probability of an event before new data is collected; the posterior probability is the statistical probability that calculates the hypothesis to be true in the light of relevant observations.

questions.q: In the weather example, P(Yes|Overcast) is computed using P(Overcast|Yes)·P(Yes)/P(Overcast). With P(Overcast|Yes)=0.44, P(Yes)=0.64, and P(Overcast)=0.29, what is P(Yes|Overcast)?
questions.e: Applying the Naive Bayes formula: P(Yes|Overcast) = 0.44 × 0.64 / 0.29 ≈ 0.98. Since this is higher than the probability of not playing, the prediction is that players will play when it is overcast.

questions.q: What does the argmax operation do in a Naive Bayes classifier?
o: It returns the smallest probability
It returns the class with the highest (maximum) probability as the output
It normalizes the probabilities to sum to 1
It computes the prior probability
questions.e: Argmax gives the class with the highest probability; for example, if P(Yes)=0.7 and P(No)=0.3, argmax outputs the class with the maximum value (Yes).

questions.q: What is a Bayesian network?
o: A single decision tree
A graphical model (a directed acyclic graph) that represents relationships between variables, where nodes are variables and arrows represent conditional probabilities/dependencies
A clustering algorithm
A method for feature scaling
questions.e: A Bayesian network is a graphical model used to represent and analyze relationships between variables; it is a directed acyclic graph in which each node represents a variable (with a probability distribution) and the arrows represent conditional probabilities, indicating how one variable depends on its parent variables.

questions.q: In a Bayesian network, what does each node store, and what is it called?
o: A feature vector; a support vector
A conditional probability table (CPT), whose values are based on experimental data
A decision boundary; a hyperplane
A cluster centroid; a mean point
questions.e: In a Bayesian network, each node (variable) has a conditional probability table (CPT) whose values are based on experimental data; the CPT of a dependent variable depends on the values of its parent variables.

questions.q: For independent events A and B, and for mutually exclusive events A and B, what are P(A and B) and P(A or B) respectively?
o: P(A and B) = P(A)+P(B); P(A or B) = P(A)×P(B)
P(A and B) = P(A)×P(B) for independent events; P(A or B) = P(A)+P(B) for mutually exclusive events
Both equal P(A)×P(B)
Both equal P(A)+P(B)
questions.e: For independent events, P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B) (one event doesn't affect the other). For mutually exclusive events, P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) (they cannot happen at the same time). For non-mutually-exclusive events, P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A and B).

questions.q: What is the key difference between a Naive Bayes classifier and a Bayesian network?
o: Naive Bayes models dependencies; Bayesian networks assume independence
Naive Bayes assumes independence among features given the class label, while a Bayesian network explicitly models the dependencies among variables using a directed acyclic graph
They are identical
Naive Bayes is unsupervised; Bayesian networks are supervised
questions.e: A Naive Bayes classifier assumes independence among features given the class label (a strong, often unrealistic assumption) and is used for classification; a Bayesian network is a probabilistic graphical model that explicitly models dependencies among variables via a directed acyclic graph, used for inference, prediction, and decision-making.

questions.q: What is logistic (logit) regression used to model?
o: A continuous numeric output with no bounds
The probability of a certain class or event existing, such as pass/fail, win/lose, alive/dead, or healthy/sick
The clustering of unlabeled data
The variance of a dataset
questions.e: The logistic (logit) model is used to model the probability of a certain class or event existing, such as pass/fail, win/lose, alive/dead, or healthy/sick — it is used for classification despite being called 'regression'.

questions.q: What are the major assumptions of logistic regression?
o: The dependent variable is continuous; many outliers are fine
The dependent variable should be dichotomous (binary), there should be no outliers, and there should be no high correlations (multicollinearity) among the predictors
The features must be perfectly correlated
The data must be unlabeled
questions.e: The major assumptions of logistic regression are: the dependent variable should be dichotomous in nature (binary, e.g. presence vs absence), there should be no outliers in the data, and there should be no high correlations (multicollinearity) among the predictors.

questions.q: What role does the sigmoid function play in logistic regression?
o: It removes outliers from the data
It is an S-shaped function that takes any number from negative to positive infinity and squishes it into the range [0,1], converting the linear regression prediction into a probability
It computes the sum of squared errors
It clusters the data points
questions.e: The sigmoid function is an S-shaped mathematical function that takes any number from negative infinity to positive infinity and squishes it into a range between 0 and 1; in logistic regression it converts the linear regression prediction into a probability.

questions.q: In logistic regression, how is the output class determined from the probability, typically using a threshold of 0.5?
o: Values above 0.5 are projected toward 0; below 0.5 toward 1
Anything below 0.5 is projected toward 0 and anything above 0.5 is projected toward 1, giving a binary output (though the threshold can be chosen depending on the problem)
The output is always the probability itself
The threshold is always exactly 0.5 and cannot change
questions.e: The mid-line typically represents 0.5 (though it can be chosen arbitrarily depending on the problem, e.g. 0.3 or 0.6); anything below 0.5 is projected downward toward 0 and anything above 0.5 upward toward 1, so 1 and 0 are the outputs. Logistic regression also gives a probability/confidence value.

questions.q: What kind of decision boundary does logistic regression produce?
o: A curved (non-linear) boundary
A linear decision boundary (the model is linear in nature)
A circular boundary
No decision boundary at all
questions.e: The logistic regression model is linear in nature, so its decision boundary is linear; ideally a curve as a decision boundary would give better performance for some problems.

questions.q: Why is plain linear regression unsuitable for modelling a binary outcome such as 'bought a product or not'?
o: Because linear regression cannot use features
Because probabilities must lie between 0 and 1, but a linear line can predict values below 0 and above 1, which do not make sense as probabilities
Because linear regression is unsupervised
Because it requires categorical inputs
questions.e: For a binary outcome, we want to model the probability, which must lie between 0 and 1; a plain linear regression line can produce values less than 0 and greater than 1, which do not make sense as probabilities. The sigmoid function solves this by bounding the output to [0,1].

questions.q: For multi-class problems where logistic regression's binary assumption is violated, which alternatives are used?
o: Simple linear regression or polynomial regression
Multinomial logistic regression or ordinal logistic regression
K-means clustering
Naive Bayes only
questions.e: Logistic regression is designed for binary outcomes; if the dependent variable has more than two categories, alternatives such as multinomial logistic regression or ordinal logistic regression are used for multi-category outcomes.

questions.q: Which is a stated limitation of logistic regression?
o: It cannot produce probabilistic output
It assumes a linear relationship between predictors and the log odds, is sensitive to outliers and multicollinearity, and is primarily limited to binary outcomes
It is only usable for regression, never classification
It requires no data at all
questions.e: Limitations of logistic regression include: it assumes a linear relationship between the predictors and the log odds, it is sensitive to outliers, it suffers from multicollinearity issues, it requires large sample sizes, it assumes independence of observations, and it is primarily limited to binary outcomes.

questions.q: What core assumption does the K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN) algorithm make?
o: That the data follows a specific mathematical distribution
That similar things exist in close proximity — similar things are near each other
That every feature is independent
That the target variable is continuous
questions.e: The KNN algorithm assumes that similar things exist in close proximity — in other words, similar things are near to each other. It is a very simple, versatile algorithm.

questions.q: KNN is described as a non-parametric and lazy learning algorithm. What does 'non-parametric' mean here?
o: That it has no parameters to compute
That there is no assumption about the underlying data distribution — the model structure is determined from the dataset
That it cannot be used for classification
That it requires a normal distribution
questions.e: Non-parametric means there is no assumption about the underlying data distribution; the model structure is determined from the dataset itself. This is helpful because most real-world datasets do not follow theoretical mathematical assumptions.

questions.q: Which set correctly orders the steps for KNN classification?
o: Assign the point; count neighbors; take K neighbors; choose K
Choose the number K of neighbors; take the K nearest neighbors (by a distance metric); count the data points in each category among them; assign the new point to the majority category
Compute centroids; assign points; recompute; converge
Split data; train; test; evaluate
questions.e: The KNN steps are: choose the number K of neighbors (usually K=5, an odd number); take the K nearest neighbors of the new point according to a distance metric (usually Euclidean distance); among these K neighbors count the number of data points in each category; and assign the new point to the category with the most neighbors.

questions.q: Which distance metric is most commonly used in KNN?
o: Manhattan distance
Euclidean distance
Cosine distance
Hamming distance
questions.e: The most often used distance metric in KNN is the Euclidean distance between the new data point and the existing points.

questions.q: Why is K usually chosen to be an odd number in binary classification?
o: To make the algorithm faster
To have a tiebreaker when taking a majority vote among the two classes
Because even numbers are invalid
To reduce the dataset size
questions.e: In cases where we take a majority vote among labels (e.g. picking the mode in a classification problem), K is usually made an odd number to have a tiebreaker, especially for binary (two-class) classification.

questions.q: How does the choice of K affect KNN's bias and variance?
o: Small K gives high bias; large K gives high variance
A very small K (e.g. K=1) causes overfitting/high variance and unstable predictions; increasing K makes predictions more stable but eventually introduces bias/underfitting and increases test error
K has no effect on bias or variance
K only affects training time
questions.e: At low K values (e.g. K=1) there is overfitting / high variance — at K=1 the training error is zero (a point's nearest neighbor is itself) but the test error is high. As K increases, predictions become more stable and test error decreases, but beyond a certain point bias/underfitting is introduced and test error rises again; the optimal K is where the test error stabilizes at a low value.

questions.q: What is the difference between eager learners and lazy learners, and which type is KNN?
o: Eager learners store data and generalize at test time; KNN is eager
Eager learners build a generalized model before prediction; lazy learners (like KNN) do little in training and store the data, performing generalization only at prediction (test) time
They are identical; KNN is neither
Lazy learners never make predictions
questions.e: Eager learners construct a generalized model before performing prediction on new points. Lazy learners do little work in the training phase — they merely store the training dataset and wait until classification is needed, doing more work at test time to generalize based on similarity to stored training tuples. KNN is a lazy learner.

questions.q: How is bias defined in the bias-variance discussion for machine learning models?
o: The variability of predictions across datasets
A systematic error from incorrect assumptions — the error between the average model prediction and the ground truth; a high-bias model does not match the data closely (underfitting)
The error only on the test set
The number of nearest neighbors
questions.e: Bias is a systematic error that occurs due to incorrect assumptions in the ML process — the error between the average model prediction and the ground truth. A model with higher bias does not match the dataset closely (underfitting), while a low-bias model closely matches the training data. Models with high bias have low variance, and vice versa.

questions.q: In a decision tree, what are the root node, decision nodes, and leaf (terminal) nodes?
o: The root is a leaf; decision nodes never split
The root node is the most significant predictor (the top), decision nodes are sub-nodes formed by splitting, and leaf/terminal nodes are the nodes that do not split further
The root node is the smallest predictor; leaf nodes are the top
All nodes are identical
questions.e: A decision tree designates the most significant predictor as the root node; splitting forms sub-nodes called decision nodes, and the nodes that do not split further are the terminal or leaf nodes. It divides the dataset into homogeneous, non-overlapping regions.

questions.q: The decision tree uses a top-down approach that is also called what, and why?
o: A bottom-up approach; because it starts from leaves
A greedy approach; because it only considers the current node being worked on, without focusing on future nodes
A random approach; because it splits randomly
A lazy approach; because it does no training
questions.e: The decision tree follows a top-down approach that is also called a greedy approach, because it only considers the current node being worked on without focusing on future nodes; it continues running until a stop criterion (such as a minimum number of observations) is reached.

questions.q: What is the Gini Index (Gini Impurity), and how is a split chosen using it?
o: The sum of squared errors; the highest Gini split is chosen

It is calculated by subtracting the sum of the squared probabilities of each class from one (measuring the probability of a randomly selected feature being misclassified); the split giving the lowest Gini Index (most pure child nodes) is chosen
The entropy of the whole tree; the deepest split is chosen
The number of leaves; the largest tree is chosen
questions.e: The Gini Index (Gini Impurity) is calculated by subtracting the sum of the squared probabilities of each class from one; it measures the probability that a randomly selected feature is classified incorrectly. More mixed data means higher impurity and a higher Gini Index; the split that gives the lowest Gini Index (the most pure child nodes) is chosen.

questions.q: The ID3 decision-tree algorithm uses which measure to decide splits?
o: Gini Index
Entropy
Euclidean distance
Silhouette score
questions.e: The ID3 algorithm uses entropy to decide splits; entropy is a measure of randomness/impurity, and related decision-tree quantities include information gain.

questions.q: Which is a stated disadvantage of decision tree classification?
o: It cannot handle multidimensional data
Trees can become very complex (overfitted trees), may not give an optimal solution, and can return a biased solution if some class label dominates
It always requires domain knowledge
It is not understandable by humans
questions.e: Disadvantages of decision tree classification include: trees can become very complex (overfitted trees), the algorithm may not produce an optimal solution, and it may return a biased solution if some class label dominates. Its advantages include requiring no domain knowledge, being intuitive/easily understood, and handling multidimensional data.

questions.q: What kind of technique is a Random Forest, and what is its base learner?
o: A single decision tree; its base learner is a neural network
An ensemble technique that uses multiple machine learning algorithms for better prediction; its base learner is the decision tree, trained on bootstrap samples
A clustering technique; its base learner is K-means
A regression technique; its base learner is the sigmoid
questions.e: A Random Forest is an ensemble technique that uses multiple machine learning algorithms for better prediction; its base learners are decision trees, each trained on a bootstrap sample (a sample bootstrapped from a larger sample).

questions.q: How does a Random Forest produce its final prediction?
o: It averages the features of all trees
Each decision tree predicts an outcome, the votes for each predicted target are counted, and the highest-voted target is taken as the final prediction (majority voting)
It uses only the first tree's prediction
It selects the tree with the lowest error
questions.e: To make a prediction, each randomly created decision tree in the forest predicts an outcome; the votes for each predicted target are counted, and the highest-voted predicted target is taken as the final prediction — this concept is known as majority voting.

questions.q: In the Random Forest terminology, which set correctly lists the important terms?
o: Sigmoid, threshold, centroid, cluster
Entropy, Information Gain, Leaf node, Decision node, Root node
Precision, Recall, F1, AUC
Bias, Variance, Overfitting, Underfitting
questions.e: Important terms in the Random Forest / decision tree context are Entropy, Information Gain, Leaf node, Decision node, and Root node.

questions.q: A decision tree is a supervised learning algorithm that works with which kinds of variables?
o: Only discrete variables
Only continuous variables
Both discrete and continuous variables
Only categorical labels
questions.e: A decision tree is a supervised learning algorithm that works for both discrete and continuous variables; it splits the dataset into subsets on the basis of the most significant attribute.

questions.q: What is clustering, and what type of learning is it?
o: A supervised task using labeled data to predict categories
An unsupervised learning task that divides data points into groups such that points in the same group are similar to each other and dissimilar to points in other groups
A regression task predicting continuous values
A reinforcement learning task using rewards
questions.e: Clustering is an unsupervised learning method (drawing references from datasets of input data without labeled responses); it is the task of dividing data points into groups such that points in the same group are more similar to each other and dissimilar to points in other groups, determining the intrinsic grouping in unlabeled data.

questions.q: In the K-means algorithm, how are data points assigned to clusters, and how are new centroids computed?
o: Points are assigned randomly; centroids are the first data points
Each point is assigned to its closest centroid (usually by Euclidean distance); new centroids are computed as the average (center of gravity) of all points in each cluster
Points are assigned by majority vote; centroids never change
Points are assigned by entropy; centroids are the medians
questions.e: In K-means, each data point is assigned to the closest centroid (usually using Euclidean distance); then new centroids are computed for each cluster as the average or center of gravity of all the points in that cluster. This is repeated until no points are reassigned — the algorithm has converged.

questions.q: When does the K-means algorithm stop (converge)?
o: After exactly K iterations
When no data points need to be reassigned to a different cluster
When the WCSS reaches its maximum
When every point is its own cluster
questions.e: The K-means algorithm converges when, after recomputing the centroids, no data point needs to be reassigned to a different cluster.

questions.q: What is a major drawback of the standard K-means algorithm, and how does K-means++ address it?
o: It is too slow; K-means++ removes points

K-means is sensitive to the initialization of the centroids (poor initialization gives poor clustering); K-means++ provides a smarter initialization by selecting each next centroid with probability proportional to its distance from the nearest already-chosen centroid
It cannot handle more than two clusters; K-means++ adds clusters
It requires labels; K-means++ removes the need for labels
questions.e: A major drawback of standard K-means is that it is sensitive to the initialization of the centroids — a poorly initialized centroid can end up with no points, or two centroids can fall in the same cluster, giving poor clustering. K-means++ addresses this with a smarter initialization: it selects the first centroid randomly, then selects each next centroid with probability proportional to its distance from the nearest previously chosen centroid; the rest of the algorithm is the same.

questions.q: What metric is used to evaluate different numbers of clusters in K-means, and how does it change as K increases?
o: The silhouette score, which increases with K
The Within Cluster Sum of Squares (WCSS), which decreases as the number of clusters K increases (reaching zero when the number of clusters equals the number of data points)
The entropy, which stays constant
The Gini Index, which increases with K
questions.e: The Within Cluster Sum of Squares (WCSS) is used to compare solutions for different values of K; it starts high and decreases as K increases, because with more centroids each point is closer to its centroid. The maximum number of clusters equals the number of data points, at which point WCSS reaches zero.

questions.q: What is the elbow method used for in K-means clustering?
o: To speed up the algorithm
To determine the optimal number of clusters by finding the point on the WCSS-vs-K curve where the decrease in WCSS goes from substantial to not substantial
To initialize the centroids
To evaluate classification accuracy
questions.e: The elbow method determines the optimal number of clusters by plotting WCSS against K: WCSS decreases sharply at first and then levels off, and the optimal K is the point (the 'elbow') where the change in WCSS goes from being substantial to not substantial.

questions.q: What are the two main types of clustering algorithm?
o: Naive Bayes and KNN
K-means clustering and hierarchical clustering
Decision trees and random forests
Linear and logistic regression
questions.e: The two clustering algorithms named are K-means clustering and hierarchical clustering.

questions.q: What does the Silhouette Coefficient measure, and what is its range?
o: Classification accuracy; range [0,100]

The separation distance between clusters (using the mean intra-cluster distance and the mean nearest-cluster distance); it ranges from -1 to 1, where higher (closer to +1) means better separation, 0 means the sample is on the boundary, and negative means it may be in the wrong cluster
The number of clusters; range [1,K]
The training error; range [0,1]
questions.e: The Silhouette Coefficient studies the separation distance between clusters, calculated using the mean of the intra-cluster distance and the nearest-cluster distance; it ranges from [-1, 1]. Higher values (closer to +1) indicate more separation between clusters, 0 indicates the sample is on or very close to the decision boundary, and a negative value indicates the sample may have been assigned to the wrong cluster.

questions.q: Which of the following are the three named clustering evaluation metrics?
o: Precision, Recall, and F1 score
Silhouette score, Calinski-Harabaz index, and Davies-Bouldin index
Accuracy, AUC, and specificity
WCSS, entropy, and Gini index
questions.e: The three commonly used clustering evaluation metrics are the Silhouette score, the Calinski-Harabaz index, and the Davies-Bouldin index.
